The Role of Gender in Digital SMS Language:  Insights from University Students

Mahnoor Channa, Abdul Malik Abbasi

This is a preprint; it has not been peer reviewed by a journal.

https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9677698/v1

This work is licensed under a CC BY 4.0 License

Abstract

This study explores gender differences in the use of linguistic features in digital SMS text messaging among students at university. As more people are relying on mobile communication, and particularly the youths. Text messaging has emerged as a style of communication. The study investigates how male and female students differ in the words they use, writing styles and use of linguistic characteristics abbreviations, emojis, repetitions, code-mixing, punctuations, and emotional expressions. In the research on language, quantitative study approach was applied in the given research. characteristics. In 30 digital SMS interactions, data was collected in 15 male and 15 interactions. students who were female and had 4 or more interactions in each interaction. The results revealed the evident differences between the male and female students. The texts of the female students were casual, emotional, and expressive. They often employed code-mixing, abbreviated words, and extended spellings in expressing emotions. They were rife with repetition, grammatical mistakes, and informal grammar, but their messages were delivered in a way that gave the impression that they were very close, funny, and had some emotional attachment as opposed to focusing on the correctness of their message. Women would be more emotive using more emojis, politeness features, adjectives, and intensifiers and tend to stretch words such as soooo or happyyy. Generally, they were more emotional, polite and expressive in their texting style compared to the male students. The male students text messages were short and informal and aimed at friendship building. They also used words such as bro, yar or bhe to express affiliation and friendship in addition to having a lot of abbreviations. Their dialogue appeared to be informal and natural because they often changed languages between Urdu and English. They put more stress using repetition of an entire word e.g., ‘okay okay’ or ‘don't worry’ ‘don't worry’ and not merely extending individual letters. The spellings and non-standard forms such as ‘gud, pleez’, or ‘becaz’ were frequent. When compared to female students, they tended to text much faster, less professionally and with more attention to connection and mutual respect. The study contributes to the research in sociolinguistics in that it presents the impact of gender in the communication style within a virtual environment. It also brings out the effects of academic setting and culture on the way students communicate through the use of text. The findings may be useful for future research on digital language practices, communication patterns, and gender-related variations in language use.
